extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policymakers, NIH staff, and others interested in the reliability and process of NIH grant peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practices for evaluating NIH R01 grant applications (preliminary ratings, written critiques, reviewer roles, and reliability metrics), including recommended calibration/training and statistical approaches for assessing interrater agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH review criteria (Significance, Innovation, Investigators, Approach, Environment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers prepared written critiques that detailed perceived strengths and weaknesses in terms of the overall impact and five specific criteria: significance, innovation, investigators, approach, and environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers assign numeric ratings for the overall impact and for each of the five specific criteria using the NIH template; critiques should address strengths and weaknesses relative to these criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall impact score
rubrics_metrics.description: An overall impact rating is assigned to each application (using the reverse 9-point scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary individual overall impact ratings are later discussed in study section meetings and final ratings from all members are averaged into a priority score used by advisory councils to make funding recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse 9-point numeric rating scale (1 = exceptional, 9 = poor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric ratings use NIH’s reverse 9-point scale with 1 representing exceptional and 9 representing poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary ratings are assigned by individual reviewers prior to meeting; higher numeric values represent more negative evaluations. Final ratings from all panel members are averaged into a priority score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written critiques listing strengths and weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Written critiques should enumerate strengths and weaknesses of the application; the study coded critiques by the number of strengths and the number of weaknesses mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques follow the NIH template and may distinguish between 'major' and all strengths/weaknesses; number and nature of strengths/weaknesses are used to relate verbal evaluations to numeric ratings and to assess reviewer agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary/secondary/tertiary reviewer roles and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically three reviewers are assigned to an application (primary, secondary, tertiary), with the primary reviewer having the expertise most closely aligned and providing the most detailed critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary reviewers produce longer, more detailed critiques and their critiques are often the focus of analysis; assignments are made based on reviewers’ biosketches and expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review based on scientific merit alone (no funding considerations during rating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers in study sections are prohibited from discussing or considering issues related to funding and are encouraged to rate each application based on scientific merit alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratings should focus on scientific quality and impact rather than funding logistics or priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premeeting preparation and submission timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are expected to read assigned applications before the meeting (applications were made available 5 weeks prior) and upload their written critiques and numeric ratings via an online portal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers in the study had access to other reviewers' submissions 2 days before the meeting; Scientific Review Officer monitors submission completeness and timeliness — adherence to timeline emulates NIH practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to discriminate excellent from good (desired evaluative sensitivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The peer-review process is expected to reliably differentiate very best applications from comparatively weaker ones (i.e., distinguish excellent from good within a pool of high-quality applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discriminative ability is a key desideratum for allocating scarce funds; the paper shows reviewers struggled to reliably make these distinctions for high-quality applications, indicating subjectivity in evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrater agreement metric: Intraclass correlation (ICC)
rubrics_metrics.description: ICC measures how strongly units within a group resemble one another; for this study, ICC indicates the extent to which different reviewers agreed in their evaluations of a single grant application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICC is computed from variance components (variance of application random intercept divided by total variance); values near zero indicate no agreement. Note: ICC cannot be negative (lower bound reported as 0), and bootstrapped CIs are used for inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrater agreement metric: Krippendorff’s alpha
rubrics_metrics.description: Krippendorff’s alpha is an interrater reliability statistic that accommodates any data type, allows missing values, and can be applied to any number of raters; it was used to assess agreement on ratings, strengths, and weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alpha values above ~0.7 are generally considered acceptable reliability; near-zero values indicate no agreement. Bootstrapping can provide 95% CIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity score (within-application vs between-application absolute differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: A similarity score computed as the difference between the average absolute difference among ratings for the same application and the average absolute difference between those ratings and ratings for other applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive values indicate that an application's ratings are more similar to each other than to ratings for other applications; tested with one-sample t-tests across applications to assess agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical modeling standards for clustered reviewer/application data (adaptive centering and LMEM with crossed random effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: When predictors vary within reviewers and within applications, adaptively center predictors (subtract reviewer mean and application mean, add grand mean) and use linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and slopes for both reviewers and applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptive/double centering separates within-cluster and between-cluster effects; LMEMs should include appropriate random effects to account for crossed nonindependence. Practical issues include convergence — removal of covariances among random effects may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine relationship between numeric ratings and written critiques (weakness/rating mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether numeric ratings correspond to the number (and magnitude) of weaknesses and strengths cited in critiques at three levels: within reviewer/application, within reviewer across applications, and across reviewers for same application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include cluster-mean predictors to decompose within-within, within-between, and between-within relationships; focus on weaknesses when strengths were not predictive. Lack of consistent mapping across reviewers indicates subjective use of the rating scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer calibration and training (score calibration talk / explicit instructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interventions such as short online training or explicit instructions that define how quantity and magnitude of weaknesses align with particular ratings are recommended to improve interrater consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior work suggests score-calibration talk influences variability; training has been shown to improve interrater reliability in some studies and is proposed as a practical remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modified lottery as an alternative allocation method
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed alternative: screen applications by reviewers and enter a proportion of top-rated applications into a lottery for funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A modified lottery could reduce costs and random components of final allocation, but requires further study (e.g., to compare downstream research impact of randomly-chosen high-rated vs slightly lower-rated applications) before implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and deidentification requirements for applications
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH peer review is confidential and review materials are destroyed after meetings; applications must be deidentified (names, institutions, contacts replaced with pseudonyms) to preserve confidentiality when emulating the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deidentification methods should preserve gender/nationality distributions if relevant; adherence to confidentiality is required to accurately emulate NIH procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection and assignment standards (expertise matching using biosketch/RePORTER)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are selected and assigned to applications based on expertise using NIH RePORTER and reviewers’ biosketches/CVs; SRO (Scientific Review Officer) manages appointments to panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matching reviewer expertise to applications is standard practice to ensure relevance of critiques and ratings; assignment is not entirely random due to specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority score calculation and use in funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Final ratings from all study section members are averaged into a final 'priority score' that advisory councils use, along with written critiques, to make funding recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority score is a central numeric summary used in subsequent funding deliberations; variability in preliminary ratings can propagate into these priority scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for reviewer verbosity via major vs all strengths/weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure verbosity does not explain disagreement, analyses can be repeated using only major strengths and major weaknesses rather than all mentioned strengths/weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study, restricting to major strengths/weaknesses produced similar low agreement, indicating verbosity was not the primary driver of disagreement.
